KEY MESSAGE 1...Sunny with light winds today. Cold again tonight 
with clear skies and light to calm winds.

High pressure continues overspreading the region today with 
yesterday's/last night's colder airmass shifting out of the region, 
along with the upper level trough that's impacted the region over 
the last few days. With 925 mb temperatures returning closer to 5C 
and yesterday's cold air advection having come to an end, highs will 
reach the 50s. Winds also remain light through the day and into 
tonight with high pressure firmly in place overhead. Skies remain 
clear through tonight, allowing for another good night of 
radiational cooling; lows tonight will dip into the 30s and upper 
20s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Mainly dry for the upcoming work week, except near 
coastal areas. Modest warming trend as high pressure builds in over 
the northeastern US.

The general trend this week is a drier, somewhat warmer pattern 
developing as a broad ridge of high pressure settles over much of 
the northeastern US and into Ontario. Temperatures moderate through 
the week with highs generally in the 50s and 60s, with cool nights 
in the 30s and 40s. The only exception to this overall trend is a 
chance for showers towards the Cape and Islands this week. 

A non-tropical low pressure developing along the cold front from 
Friday night settles just offshore of the Carolina coastal waters. 
The aforementioned front looks to have stalled out and a bit of 
upper level energy from the associated trough broke away and drifted 
to that same area, aiding in the development of this low pressure. 
Latest HREF members have shown some of the showers associated with 
the northern precipitation shield of this low making their way up to 
southeastern parts of New England, mainly the Cape and Islands, 
finding a weak point in the ridge aloft. Some of the global 
deterministic guidance agrees, indicating some showers making their 
way over the Cape and Islands. Though across all models, QPF remains 
quite low. Latest global guidance (ensemble and deterministic) have 
also trended down on rain chances later this week. Despite minimal 
impacts in terms of rain expected with this low pressure, marine 
impacts are looking a bit more significant as it remains relatively 
stationary over the same area, churning over the same waters for 
what appears to be most of this week. This will lead to seas up to 
15-17 ft offshore of Nantucket.
 
The gradient between this area of low pressure and the 
aforementioned high pressure over the northeast US will tighten 
greatly, increasing ENE winds over the waters and towards the Cape 
and Islands, RI, and the coastal plain in SE MA. These start to 
really build up towards Monday night as the low pressure deepens and 
drifts very slightly north. Ensembles have continued to indicate 
decent probabilities of sustained winds reaching gale-force over the 
southern waters, with the GEFS and Canadian ensemble up to 30-40% 
(and even up to 70% in the Canadian guidance over the ocean waters) 
just south of the Islands. In terms of gale-force gusts, 
probabilities have remained somewhat steady compared to the last 
update, remaining in the high (80-100%) range in the ECMWF ensemble 
and up to 80% in the GEFS. However, there was a bit of a southward 
shift of the core of the highest sustained gale probabilities. This 
lines up with the majority of members across the ensemble suites 
tracking the center of this low pressure well to the south and east 
of the 40N/70W benchmark. Persistent easterly fetch associated with 
these winds, along with building rough seas, will need to be 
monitored as well, as beach erosion for east- and northeast-facing 
beaches may become an issue.

Towards the end of the week, ensembles indicate troughing from 
Canada making a pass towards southern New England, which would aid 
in steering this low pressure out to sea. Significant ridging aloft 
over much of the CONUS looks to persist and even intensify, then 
becomes more tilted towards the Great Lakes region towards the 
weekend. This would be associated with a strong Canadian high 
pressure that looks to strengthen over the northeast after 
originating from the Canadian Prairies, which would lean towards 
drier conditions for the whole region once again.
